Prevention: Grow resistant/ tolerant varieties whenever possible (Ana (2300-3000masl), dorset golden (>2800 masl) and
When planting use appropriate spacing, 3m x 3m is recommended when planting apple trees
Regular pruning will improve free air circulation and sunlight penetration - this will help the canopy to dry more quickly and make the tissues less susceptible to the disease
Burn/bury fallen infected leaves, flowers, and rotten fruits on which immature fungal structure can 'over winter' and spead the infection next season
Restrict movement of branches, above ground stems, shoots, fruits from infected areas in to areas where the disease is not present
Monitoring: This fungal disease attacks the leaves, flowers, petioles (leaf stalks) and fruits but symptoms are most obvious on the leaves and fruits
Regularly check leaves when they start to emerge.
Check for lesions on both sides but particularly the undersides
Lesions appear on leaves as small light brown/ olive green spots which eventually turn dark brown/black.
As they get larger they distort the shape of the leaves
Lesions on young fruit enlarge to form brown corky spots (scabs).
This can cause fruit infected early in the season to crack and infected fruits often drop prematurely
Fruit infected close to maturity develop small black circular spots or pits - often in storage
Direct Control: Remove scabby fruits from the trees and orchard floor and destroy as they often become primary sources of inoculum
Remove dead branches and twigs from the orchard and destroy to prevent spreading the disease as it can survive on dead material for a long time
Restrictions: There are no registered fungicides in
Ethiopia for the management of this disease
